notes.meaning: The fight between Saul's family and David's family dragged on for years. It was more a state of hostility than nonstop battles, because neither side would recognize the other's king. Over time more and more people turned to David as the king God had chosen. The long wait tested David's faith and patience. Matthew Henry also sees a picture here of God's grace slowly growing stronger in a believer while sin grows weaker.

While David ruled in Hebron, six sons were born to him, each by a different mother. The list shows David's house growing stronger, while Saul's house was shrinking. Still, Matthew Henry says having many wives went against God's law for kings (Deuteronomy 17:17). Three of these sons, Amnon, Absalom and Adonijah, later brought David great grief. Marrying Maacah, a foreign king's daughter, seems to have been a political move to gain an ally, and it led to the troubled life of Absalom. Chileab is also called Daniel in 1 Chronicles 3:1.

Abner, the army commander, was the real power behind Saul's son Ish-bosheth. Ish-bosheth accused him of sleeping with Rizpah. She was a concubine, a kind of secondary wife, of the late King Saul. In that world, taking a dead king's concubine was a way of claiming his throne. The Bible does not tell us whether the charge was true.

Abner exploded in anger. "Am I the head of a dog?" means "Do you think I'm worthless, after all I've done for your family?" He reminded Ish-bosheth that he alone had kept him from falling to David. Matthew Henry notes that Abner never actually denies the charge, and that proud people often refuse to accept correction.

Abner swore he would now hand the whole kingdom over to David, "from Dan to Beersheba," meaning the whole land from north to south. His words show he had known God's promise to David all along, yet he had fought against it. His ambition first drove him to serve Ish-bosheth, and now revenge drove him to serve David. Even so, God used Abner's anger to carry out His own plan.
Ish-bosheth was too afraid to answer. He was a weak king who really depended on his general. Adam Clarke notes how sad it is for a ruler to be at the mercy of the man who commands his army.

Abner sent messengers to make a deal with David. "To whom does the land belong?" means "Isn't it rightly yours, by God's choice?" Wesley says God can overrule the passions of wicked men to do His own wise work.

David agreed, but only if Abner brought back Michal, Saul's daughter and David's first wife. Matthew Henry sees real love here, and respect for Saul's family. Other commentators think David also had a political reason: having Saul's daughter as his wife would help win over Saul's supporters. Michal was his lawful wife, taken from him by force.

David formally asked Ish-bosheth to return Michal. Ish-bosheth's consent was needed, and this made the handover a public act. David reminded him of the bride-price Saul had set: a hundred Philistine foreskins (1 Samuel 18). Wesley thinks this request also gave Ish-bosheth some hope of peace with David.

Michal was taken from Paltiel, the man Saul had given her to. He followed her, weeping, as far as Bahurim, near Judah's border, until Abner sent him home. His grief is painful to read. But Matthew Henry notes he had married a woman he knew belonged to another man. Clarke adds that David still had the legal right to her, since she had never been divorced.

Abner urged the leaders of Israel to make David their king. He reminded them they had wanted David before, and that God had promised to save Israel through him. What he said about David's calling was true. But commentators say he acted out of revenge against Ish-bosheth while pretending to have religious motives. Clarke notes that the exact promise Abner quotes is not recorded elsewhere in Scripture.

Abner made a special effort with the tribe of Benjamin. It was Saul's own tribe, and the one most likely to resist losing the crown. Benjamin was also strong and lay between Judah and the other tribes, so winning it over was key. Then Abner went to Hebron to report to David.
Abner came to Hebron with twenty men, and David gave them a feast. The meal sealed their agreement and showed that the two men were now at peace.

Abner promised to gather all Israel to make a covenant, a binding agreement, with David as king. David sent him away in peace and in good faith, with no plan to harm him. Matthew Henry sees here a good example of living at peace, even with people whose motives are mixed.

Just then Joab, David's army commander, came back from a raid with a lot of plunder. The raid was probably against Philistines or other raiders who were attacking Judah during the unrest. Abner had already left in peace.
When Joab arrived, he was told that Abner had visited the king and had been sent off in peace. Matthew Henry notes that Joab learned that many friendly words had passed between the two.

Joab rudely scolded the king and claimed Abner had only come to spy. Joab may have truly doubted Abner. But he had other reasons too. Abner was a skilled general who might replace him, and Abner had killed Joab's brother Asahel. Matthew Henry is amazed both at Joab's nerve and at David's patience.
Behind David's back, Joab sent messengers to bring Abner back, probably using the king's name. David knew nothing about it. Abner, meaning no harm, suspected none.

Joab pulled Abner aside at the city gate, as if to talk privately, and stabbed him. He claimed to be avenging Asahel. But Abner had killed Asahel in battle, in self-defense, after warning him, so this was not lawful revenge. It was a treacherous murder, done in peacetime and in the open gate where justice was supposed to be done. It was also an attack on David's own plans.

When David heard, he solemnly declared before God that he and his kingdom were innocent of Abner's blood. He wanted no one to think he had secretly ordered it. Matthew Henry says it is a comfort to be able to say honestly that we had no part in a wrong.

David called down a curse on Joab's family: lasting disease, weakness, violent death and hunger. Murder brings a curse on families, and if people do not punish it, God will. Matthew Henry and Wesley ask whether firmly punishing Joab himself would have been better than cursing his descendants. Clarke notes the words can also be read as a prediction of what would happen.

The writer adds that Joab and his brother Abishai both murdered Abner. Joab struck the blow, but Abishai shared the guilt because he agreed to it and supported it. Their excuse was Asahel's death, but Abner had killed Asahel in self-defense in battle.

David ordered everyone, including Joab, to tear their clothes and wear sackcloth, rough cloth worn in grief. Making Joab mourn publicly put him to shame and called him to repentance. King David himself walked behind the bier, the frame that carried the body. This was unusual for a king, but it honored Abner and showed David had no part in the killing.
Abner was buried in Hebron, and the king wept aloud at the grave, and all the people wept with him. Though Abner had been his enemy, David's grief was real and deep.

David sang a short lament, a song of grief. The word for "fool" here means a worthless or wicked man, like Nabal in 1 Samuel 25. Abner did not die like a criminal, tied up and executed by justice. He was tricked and cut down by wicked men. The song was both sorrow and a sharp rebuke to Joab, and it made the people weep even more.

The people urged David to eat, but he vowed to fast until sunset. Going without food was how deep mourners showed their grief in that time. Matthew Henry notes how fitting it is to keep a house of mourning from turning into a house of feasting.

The people saw that David's grief was sincere, and they were pleased. All Israel became convinced that the king had no part in Abner's murder. David's conduct even turned public opinion in his favor, more honorably than Abner's scheming would have. Matthew Henry adds that a willingness to please, and to be pleased, makes any relationship happy.

David called Abner a great prince who had fallen. He could not call him a good man, so he praised what was true: his rank and his ability. Abner died just as he was doing his most useful work. Wesley notes how small death makes even the mighty.

David admitted he was weak. He was newly made king, and Joab and Abishai, the sons of his sister Zeruiah, were too powerful for him to punish safely. So he left their punishment to the Lord. Matthew Henry and Wesley say he should have done justice and trusted God with the outcome; sparing Joab may have led to more murders later. David finally left the matter to Solomon. Spurgeon applies the verse to believers: the very strengths we lean on can become our hindrances.
